summary:
Reuters-sourced news item, republished by Allwork.Space, reporting that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is reviewing AI companies' corporate disclosures amid investor concern about a possible AI bubble inflated by circular deals. SEC enforcement director David Woodcock, who took the role in May, told Reuters the agency does not want to impede tech innovation but must ensure issuers give investors a full picture of material risks. He said the principal concern is accurate disclosure of material information, and that where disclosure fails, enforcement will be present.

Context: Big Tech stocks sold off during the week after companies disclosed heavy cash burn funding AI expansion at a time of rising interest rates, prompting questions about the sustainability of AI spending.

Woodcock also warned that AI and superintelligence have made scams cheaper and easier to manufacture at scale, increasing risk exposure for more people. He said brokers and other firms need processes to protect retail investors and take thoughtful action.

On private markets, Woodcock said the enforcement team's asset management unit is focused on conflicts of interest and valuations, and predicted more activity in that space. Reuters previously reported the SEC was probing a type of private equity fund as part of broader interest in opaque markets.

On prediction markets, which let users bet on real-world events including sports, policy announcements and elections, Woodcock said the SEC has an oversight role. The markets, led by Polymarket and Kalshi, have surged over the past two years and are pushing into US stocks; equity-linked prediction markets would traditionally fall under SEC jurisdiction. Enforcement staff are coordinating with policy officials and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees swap markets. Woodcock said the agency does not want to regulate the new industry through enforcement actions, preferring involvement that does not crush innovation.

The piece is capital-markets regulation news with no workplace, facilities or workplace-tech operational content.
